title: Washington Crosses the Delaware
text:
By December 1776 the American cause seemed close to collapse. George Washington's army had been driven out of New York and chased across New Jersey into Pennsylvania. It had shrunk to a few thousand ill-clothed men, and most of their enlistments would expire on 31 December. Thomas Paine wrote that these were the times that try men's souls.

Washington decided to strike before his army dissolved. Across the Delaware River, at Trenton, New Jersey, a garrison of Hessian soldiers under Colonel Johann Rall held an advanced post for the winter. On the night of 25 December, Washington took about 2,400 men across the icy river at McConkey's Ferry, in a storm of snow and sleet, with artillery hauled in boats. The crossing ran hours late, and two supporting columns failed to cross at all. Washington went ahead anyway.

The soldiers marched about nine miles through the storm and attacked Trenton from two directions early on the morning of 26 December. The Hessians, caught by surprise, tried to form up in the streets under American cannon fire. Rall was mortally wounded, and around nine hundred Hessians surrendered. The Americans lost only a handful of men.

A week later Washington won again at Princeton. The victories revived the morale of the army and the country, and enough soldiers agreed to stay on to keep the revolution alive.
lesson: At your lowest point, a well-chosen, limited success can restore belief. Pick a target you can actually win, and act before the moment passes.
people: George Washington, Johann Rall, Henry Knox
location: Delaware River and Trenton, New Jersey (USA)
source: Washington's letters and reports to Congress; David Hackett Fischer, Washington's Crossing (2004)
place: Trenton Battle Monument, Trenton, New Jersey, USA
